requirements.name: composer image attachment entrypoints
key UX: The chat composer lets users attach one or more local images from phone or desktop without leaving the current thread flow.

The image-attachment entrypoint is placed in the same action column area that contains New Thread and Rollback so the attachment affordance stays near primary thread actions instead of being buried inside the text input.
Selected images appear as removable attachment chips or thumbnails before send so users can verify exactly what will be submitted.
A text-only message, image-only message, or mixed text-plus-image message can all be submitted from the same composer surface.
requirements.design detail: The product should add a dedicated image-picker action in the vertical action area alongside New Thread and Rollback, not as an extension of the current composer input row. Tapping the action opens a new purpose-built attachment dialog owned by this feature rather than stretching the existing UI shell. The local draft model must expand from text-only to a structured content list so text and attachments are first-class peers.

requirements.name: server-managed persistent attachment storage
key UX: Attached images are stored by My-Code-X in a stable local attachment area instead of relying on browser memory, temp files, or workspace pollution.
The same attachment remains resolvable during send, stream, resume, and later thread hydration as long as the retention policy has not expired.
Users do not need to understand local file paths; attachment persistence is invisible and reliable.
requirements.design detail: Persist attachments under an application-owned root outside the workspace, for example `%USERPROFILE%/.my-code-x/attachments/...` on Windows. Saved files must use absolute paths so `turn/start` can pass them to Codex as `localImage`. The storage layout should include date-based sharding plus stable ids to avoid collisions and support cleanup.

requirements.name: pre-send compression with clarity-first image standard
key UX: Very large user images are compressed automatically before Codex sees them, reducing upload and inference cost without making screenshots or text unreadable.
Images that are already reasonably sized are kept visually unchanged instead of being recompressed unnecessarily.
Compression failures fall back to a clear user-facing error instead of silently sending a broken or empty attachment.
Reasonably large images are compressed, while uploads that exceed a system-protection hard cap are rejected explicitly instead of consuming unbounded decode or compression resources.
requirements.design detail: Adopt one fixed server-side canonicalization standard instead of trying to classify images by content. Step 0: enforce a raw-upload safety hard cap and decoded-pixel safety cap before expensive processing so pathological files are rejected early for system protection; this hard cap is distinct from the normal compression path and must not reject ordinary large photos or screenshots that can be normalized safely. Step 1: normalize orientation from EXIF and strip metadata. Step 2: if the file exceeds 2 MB or its longest edge exceeds 1600 px, resize proportionally so the longest edge becomes 1600 px. Step 3: encode the persisted attachment with a single default lossy profile such as JPEG quality 85 when the source has no transparency, and a single transparency-safe profile such as WebP quality 92 or PNG fallback when transparency must be preserved. Step 4: enforce a saved target of 2 MB or less per attachment; if still above cap after the first pass, re-encode once more at the same 1600 px bound with a slightly lower quality floor before rejecting. The rule is intentionally simple and deterministic: every large user image is normalized to the same AI-friendly bound, and screenshots, UI captures, logs, and code snippets must remain legible at normal mobile transcript width.

requirements.name: structured send pipeline using localImage inputs
key UX: When the user sends a message with attachments, the turn reaches Codex as one structured input list containing text plus one `localImage` item per saved attachment.
The same structured content is reflected immediately in the local transcript so the message preview matches what Codex actually received.
The send API rejects malformed attachment references early rather than producing partial or ambiguous turns.
requirements.design detail: Replace the current text-only `/api/v2/chat/message` payload with a structured content contract. The server validates attachment ids, resolves them to persisted files, and builds `turn/start.input` as ordered items such as `text` followed by `localImage`. Local optimistic transcript state must store the same structured content, not just a derived plain-text summary.

requirements.name: transcript rendering for attached user images
key UX: User messages with image attachments show actual thumbnails in the transcript instead of generic `[image]` or `[localImage]` placeholders.
Mixed messages preserve ordering so text and images appear in the same sequence the user composed.
Users can tap an attachment to inspect it at a larger size without losing chat context.
requirements.design detail: The transcript renderer should treat user message `content[]` as displayable structured content. Text remains markdown-capable where appropriate, and image attachments render via a server-backed image URL rather than exposing raw local filesystem paths to the browser.

requirements.name: safe server image serving for transcript and resume
key UX: Previously sent attachments still render after refresh or thread resume as long as the retained local file exists.
The browser never receives unrestricted filesystem access or arbitrary path reads.
Broken or expired attachments degrade to a clear unavailable state instead of crashing transcript rendering.
requirements.design detail: Add a dedicated authenticated image read route that serves only app-managed attachment files by attachment id. The route must resolve ids through attachment metadata, not direct client-supplied paths. Missing files should return a controlled not-found response so the UI can show an explicit unavailable attachment state.

requirements.name: attachment validation and guardrails
key UX: Unsupported files are rejected before send with a specific reason, such as unsupported type or image too large to process.
Users cannot accidentally attach an unlimited number of huge files in one turn.
A single message can contain at most 5 image attachments, and attempts to exceed that limit are blocked with a clear limit message.
Malformed uploads, path traversal attempts, or non-image payloads are blocked at the server boundary.
requirements.design detail: Accept common web-safe image sources such as JPEG, PNG, WebP, and optionally HEIC when the server stack can decode it reliably. Enforce a hard cap of 5 attachments per message plus caps for raw upload size and decoded pixel count. The server must sniff actual MIME or decode capability rather than trusting extension alone.

requirements.name: attachment draft lifecycle and picker workflow
key UX: When users tap the image action, they enter a dedicated attachment dialog instead of an expanded version of the existing composer UI.
The dialog shows selected images in the order they will be sent, supports removing individual images before send, and makes the 5-image cap obvious.
An attachment remains in a draft lifecycle state such as processing, ready, failed, or removed so users can understand whether the message is sendable.
requirements.design detail: Define an attachment-draft state machine for selected images before message send. The dedicated dialog belongs to the chat image attachments feature and is responsible for file picking, draft preview, per-item status, removal, and limit messaging. First version behavior should keep ordering equal to selection order and does not need drag-and-drop reordering.

requirements.name: processing and send status feedback
key UX: Each selected image shows a clear draft status such as processing, ready, failed, or removed so users can tell whether the message can be sent.
The send action is blocked whenever any selected attachment is still processing or has failed, preventing partial or ambiguous turns.
When attachment processing or message send fails, the UI shows a specific error state and lets users remove the failed image or retry the whole send without reselecting successful attachments.
requirements.design detail: Define explicit send gating and feedback rules. While any attachment is in processing, the send action must stay disabled and the dialog should indicate that preparation is still running. If any attachment enters failed, the message remains unsendable until the failed item is removed or successfully reprocessed. After all attachments are ready, sending the message transitions the draft into a sending state. If the final message send fails after attachment preparation succeeded, the prepared attachments remain in the draft so the user can retry the send directly without picking files again. First version should treat attachment readiness as all-or-nothing for send eligibility rather than allowing partial sends.

requirements.name: attachment lifecycle and cleanup policy
key UX: Attachments remain available for active and recent threads without requiring users to re-upload the same image after every refresh.
Old orphaned files do not grow local storage forever.
Cleanup is predictable and does not delete images that are still referenced by active chat history.
requirements.design detail: Persist attachment metadata with ownership information such as attachment id, saved path, original filename, content hash, byte sizes, image dimensions, created time, and last referenced thread ids. Implement a retention policy that keeps referenced files for active history and prunes orphaned or expired files on a scheduled maintenance path.

requirements.name: debuggability and observable compression results
key UX: When attachment processing fails, operators have enough information to diagnose whether the issue came from decode, compression, storage, or Codex handoff.
The product can report whether compression saved meaningful size on large images without exposing private image content.
Developers can verify that Codex received `localImage` inputs pointing at the persisted compressed files.
requirements.design detail: Record structured logs for attachment ingest, compression decisions, saved output dimensions, chosen codec, byte savings, and send-time path resolution. Do not log raw image bytes or browser data URLs.
